1518963184736120833 [2022-04-26] @peakexperiments  [(SEED) type=semantic_search]
I had a religious experience over a decade ago. What it did was convince me there's more in the universe than meets the eye. I'm more than just a bunch of dumb atoms moving in their dumb fated directions.

What it did not do is tell me what religion to be, what to believe.
↓
1518963186761977856 [2022-04-26] @peakexperiments 
It was as if God knocked at my door and said, "Hey dumbass, stop being a nihilist. kthxbye" and then disappeared.

↓
1518963189119127553 [2022-04-26] @peakexperiments 
I went to various churches since then but always felt pressured to believe in things I wasn't necessarily convinced of. Tried out various Eastern and other spiritual paths and ultimately felt the same. I just didn't "get into it" the way the others seemed to.
↓
1518963191392489474 [2022-04-26] @peakexperiments 
'm starting to return to the question, "Should I just stop worrying about myself and start trusting that I'm saved?"

The pros to this are holy crap I'd love this. Just to start living and stop worrying. A child of God who will return to His bosom at the right time. Chill, dude.
↓

1518963197423894531 [2022-04-26] @peakexperiments 
I suppose I ought to continue developing my conscience, regardless. Evolve my sense of right and wrong, what I can reasonably expect of myself versus what is too much to expect of any mortal. And thus evaluate honestly where I stand with my own conscience.
↓

↓

We want it, obviously, but is it actually possible for a mortal? Or does that happen only after death, if at all?

1950317131775586583 [2025-07-29] @algekalipso 💜 76 🔁 4 [(SEED) type=semantic_search]
To a first approximation, the more intense something feels, the more "real" we think it is. This is the core reason why psychedelics often cause experiences that "feel more real than real".

Yes, there are reasons to believe DMT experiences have significant epistemic value. But in practice people believe they experienced something beyond mere hallucinations due to the sheer intensity of the effects. Rather than, say, because they noticed the presence of exotic symmetry groups in their somatosensory field.

E.g. "I know Jesus is real because I have intense experiences associated with him". Not because, e.g. "there are unusual computational properties to the Jesus-imbued state of consciousness", even though the latter is objectively more impressive. You should see what I would be like as a pope...

│   "more intense" == "more real" is the very syntax of conscious perception. Many artifacts follow from this.

│   @algekalipso Listen Andrés, for years now you’ve been trying to tell me that my personal DMT familiar, Yoshimi the Great Dragon Serpahim—a hyperdimensional demigod who’s scales are smaller versions of itself—is nothing more than a series of gliding dragon-curve fractals, and I’m here for it!
│   ↓
│   1950327054810935419 [2025-07-29] @algekalipso 💜 5
│   @TheDaoOfZion Haha! I think I've remained open minded! And I hope I've made that clear. It's just that I hope we can at least try to algorithmically reduce our experiences before we jump to strong metaphysical conclusions. Even though... Well, look at me "Life Review" video 😆
└── 1950382916040613926 [2025-07-30] @tim_tyler 💜 5
    @algekalipso My model is a bit different: various neurons encode significance. Psychedelics cause some of those neurons to fire repeatedly for eight hours or so - due to associated receptors being chemically occupied. As a result, everything seems to be of great significance.
    ↓
    1950518151487107426 [2025-07-30] @algekalipso 💜 2
    I don't think it's very likely that there are specific neurons that trigger the sense of significance in the sense that the essence of significance is inside those neurons. I think more likely, just as with the pleasure centers, the phenomenon of the sense of significance (or of pleasure) is a holistic property of the state as a whole.
    
    In the Symmetry Theory of Valence, the please centers are hypothesized to be modulators of whole-brain harmony. It's the global harmony that feels good, not the activity in the pleasure centers per se. A double dissociation experiment could falsify this: induce global harmony with TMS while inhibiting the pleasure centers and we expect the state to feel good regardless; activate the pleasure centers while inhibiting the harmonic response and we'd expect that to not feel good.
    
    I think the intensity (modulating the energy parameter) is upstream of the sense of significance. Because on DMT absolutely all sensations are much more intense, yet not all of them feel as significant. Akin to Laser Chess, the centrality of a sensation is more the result of the PageRank of how sensations reference one another and where attention pools, than something inherent in them. Does that make sense? Like the PageRank of a graph, sometimes small edits to the network can have huge effects on where the PageRank pools. Same with the sense of significance in a scene. It's sort of a result of everything interacting with everything else rather than a "tag" the brain adds by default if certain neurons are activated.

rating.reasoning_summary: This strand explores the epistemic status of psychedelic experiences and their relationship to religious/spiritual belief. The boundary object is the recurring question: 'Are drug-induced spiritual experiences real knowledge or just intense hallucinations?' The arc spans from eigenrobot's 2021 poll on God vs atheism, through peakexperiments' 2022 theological uncertainty, to algekalipso's 2025 neuroscientific framework (Symmetry Theory) attempting to explain why intensity creates perceived realness. The discourse is primarily constructive rather than dialectical—people are sharing phenomenological reports and building vocabulary ('structural change,' 'PageRank of significance') rather than debating truth claims. However, the strand lacks resolution: it documents a persistent confusion rather than producing a durable framework for adjudicating spiritual experiences.

essential_tweets.annotation: The origin: eigenrobot's poll framing the choice between 'omniscient God' vs 'world bereft of Divinity' as equally difficult to grapple with, setting up the epistemic problem
The diagnostic: linking God-belief to hallucinogen use, establishing psychedelics as a vector for spiritual experience in this community
The phenomenological report: peakexperiments describes a 'religious experience' that provided certainty of non-materialism but no doctrinal clarity
The theological dilemma: should one 'trust in salvation' (complacency risk) or remain uncertain (perpetual anxiety)?
The key question formalized: are drug-induced vs non-drug spiritual experiences 'the same or different'?
First theoretical answer: experientially identical, but non-drug experiences indicate 'structural brain change' (durability criterion)
Edge case: transkatgirl reports intense psychedelic-like experiences while sober, complicating the drug/non-drug binary
The taxonomy: algekalipso's viral tweet mapping specific substances to specific religious frameworks (LSD→Hinduism, DMT→animism, 5-MeO→Buddhism)
The testimonial: sariazout's widely-shared claim that one mushroom trip exceeded 37 years of other self-improvement methods
The theoretical synthesis: algekalipso's neuroscientific explanation—intensity creates perceived realness via 'PageRank of significance,' not inherent epistemic value
